{"id": "3:64/q06", "question": "How is kalima read?", "turns_on": "The variants alter kāf or lām vowels and stillness.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q06/p1", "position": "The lām is still, with fatḥa or kasra on kāf.", "reasons": "Abu al-Sammal has both attributions; Qu'nub and Alusi mention shifting the lām's vowel, as with kabid/kabd. Abu Hayyan compares sidra and darba."}, {"id": "3:64/q06/p2", "position": "The common form has fatḥa on kāf and kasra on lām.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and al-Samin call it the basic form."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q07", "question": "What is the common word's content?", "turns_on": "Most take the ensuing clauses as its content; some compress it to the tawhid confession or read it inwardly.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q07/p1", "position": "It is worshipping God alone, associating no partner, and making no human lord.", "reasons": "The following clauses explain it; Baydawi, Nasafi and others say prophets and scriptures agree. Ibn Hisham says the appeal removes their argument."}, {"id": "3:64/q07/p2", "position": "It is the declaration 'there is no god but God'.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aliya and Mujahid name the formula; Damghani and others repeat it."}, {"id": "3:64/q07/p3", "position": "It is inward servanthood and realized divine unity.", "reasons": "Al-Wasiti invokes servanthood before divine self-sufficiency; Ibn Ata realization of unity; Qushayri God as sole originator."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q08", "question": "What does sawāʾ mean?", "turns_on": "Glosses emphasize justice, balanced middle, shared standing or shared scriptural agreement.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q08/p1", "position": "Justice, fairness, and equitable balance.", "reasons": "Zuhayr's poetry, Ibn Masud's 'word of justice,' and other Quranic uses support this. Bint al-Shati identifies equality as the root sense and distinguishes it from legal ʿadl."}, {"id": "3:64/q08/p2", "position": "The balanced middle or right course.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says the middle is fairest; commentators cite 37:55, 20:58, 38:22, 41:10 and 28:22. Ibn Atiyya calls right direction close to justice."}, {"id": "3:64/q08/p3", "position": "What Torah, Gospel and Quran agree on.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and later commentators take equality as shared scriptural meaning; Tabatabai says the following clause corrects distorted understandings."}, {"id": "3:64/q08/p4", "position": "Equal standing of all persons in a shared truth.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya prefers parity of status: a captive's choice of conversion or death may be just yet unequal, whereas faith with freedom and an equal share invites as peers. Abu Hayyan dismisses the extension; Ibn Ashur approves it. Tabatabai emphasizes equal acceptance and action."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q09", "question": "What is sawāʾ's grammatical form and reading?", "turns_on": "The common genitive adjective competes with a verbal noun analysis and al-Hasan's accusative.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q09/p1", "position": "Genitive adjective of kalima, often an adjectival verbal noun.", "reasons": "Basran grammarians, Zajjaj and the majority give this parse; a verbal noun need not agree in gender or number. Ibn Abi al-Rabi discusses its ability to raise a coordinated noun."}, {"id": "3:64/q09/p2", "position": "A noun or verbal noun of equality, with an estimated 'possessing' or adverbial sense.", "reasons": "The Kufan grammarian and Tabrisi mention a nominal parse; sawā/suwā are shortened alternate forms, illustrated by 20:58."}, {"id": "3:64/q09/p3", "position": "Al-Hasan's accusative is a cognate accusative or circumstantial modifier.", "reasons": "Al-Hawfi and Zamakhshari supply istawat istiwāʾ; al-Shaykh objects to an implied governing verb. Sibawayh permits a circumstance from an indefinite noun, which al-Samin accepts."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q10", "question": "What does 'between us and you' refer to and depend on?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q10/p1", "position": "It denotes the Prophet and Muslims opposite the invitees, and is governed by sawāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur infers 'us' from the final command; Zuhayr's verse supports the construction of sawāʾ with bayna."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q11", "question": "How is an lā naʿbuda parsed?", "turns_on": "Analyses differ over apposition, an implied subject or preposition, explanatory an, and predicate relations.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q11/p1", "position": "Genitive apposition to kalima, explaining the common word.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, Zajjaj, Wahidi and others adopt it; Ibn Ashur favors it under grammatical convention."}, {"id": "3:64/q11/p2", "position": "Nominative predicate after an implicit 'it is'.", "reasons": "Zajjaj treats it as the answer to 'What is the word?' Tabrisi discusses an lightened from emphatic an, citing 20:89 and 21:44."}, {"id": "3:64/q11/p3", "position": "Explanatory an, with prohibitive jussive or indicative verbs.", "reasons": "Zajjaj compares 43:23; Sibawayh licenses jussive or raised verbs. Al-Kisai and al-Farra invoke attraction to a supposed opening an; al-Nahhas rejects that account."}, {"id": "3:64/q11/p4", "position": "An omitted preposition yields an accusative clause.", "reasons": "Al-Thalabi and al-Jishumi supply bi-an; Baghawi also gives the analysis."}, {"id": "3:64/q11/p5", "position": "Nominative subject with baynanā as predicate.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa proposes a stop at sawāʾ; al-Akhfash and Kufans allow an unsupported adverb to govern, unlike Basrans. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin fault a missing link."}, {"id": "3:64/q11/p6", "position": "Apposition to sawāʾ.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa allows it; al-Samin calls it unclear. Ibn Hisham and Ibn Ashur reject its adjective-like result, while al-Damamini disputes their objection."}, {"id": "3:64/q11/p7", "position": "Subject governed by sawāʾ after an implied link.", "reasons": "Ali ibn Isa and al-Zamani estimate an omitted fiha; Abu Hayyan and al-Shaykh call that omission weak."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q12", "question": "What does worshipping God alone entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q12/p1", "position": "Sincere exclusive devotion to the one God.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the clause denies other objects of worship, not God's existence, and understands except-God appositionally. Razi argues worship belonged only to God before Jesus; Tabatabai grounds one Lord in one Creator."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q13", "question": "What does associating nothing with God prohibit?", "turns_on": "Some treat this as a distinct foundation and some as emphatic expansion.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q13/p1", "position": "No being can share God's worthiness of worship or divine status.", "reasons": "Wahidi explains bi as 'with'; Ibn Kathir includes idols, crosses, tyrants and fire (21:25; 16:36). Biqai excludes even an unworshipped supposed partner; Razi argues three independent hypostases entail shirk."}, {"id": "3:64/q13/p2", "position": "The added prohibition reinforces exclusive worship.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says all three negatives overlap to address deeply rooted practice; Alusi mentions emphasis but prefers an independent foundation. Tabatabai notes worship of one supposed partner remains shirk."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q14", "question": "How does 'anything' work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q14/p1", "position": "It may be object or verbal noun, with unrestricted negation.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan extends the negative over object, act, time, place and manner; Alusi rejects narrowing it to 'forms of idolatry'."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q15", "question": "What is meant by taking one another as lords?", "turns_on": "The sources distinguish deification, unauthorized obedience, bodily homage, idols, indwelling, and absolute human rule.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q15/p1", "position": "Obeying clergy or leaders against God's command, especially in lawful and forbidden rulings.", "reasons": "9:31 and Adi ibn Hatim's report say accepting clergy's reversals is worship without ritual devotion. Ibn Jurayj includes chiefs outside worship; al-Fudayl likens it to prayer away from the qibla."}, {"id": "3:64/q15/p2", "position": "Treating Jesus, Ezra, another human, or angels as divine or God's child.", "reasons": "Muqatil singles out Jesus; Ibn Abbas includes Uzayr. Zajjaj stresses Jesus' humanity; Asad mentions saints and Talmudic scholars; Elmalili argues 'teacher' does not remove the Trinity issue (3:48)."}, {"id": "3:64/q15/p3", "position": "Bowing or prostrating to one another.", "reasons": "Ikrima gives this sense; Qurtubi cites Muadh's proposed prostration and Anas' handshaking report. Razi includes prostration to clergy."}, {"id": "3:64/q15/p4", "position": "Attributing divine indwelling or independent agency to perfected or powerful humans.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim reports ascetics attributing revival and healing to spiritually perfected people; Biqai rejects independent created agency; Qushayri and Bursevi reject reliance on people for provision."}, {"id": "3:64/q15/p5", "position": "One person's absolute domination over another violates equal human standing.", "reasons": "Tabatabai reasons from shared humanity and exclusive divine lordship; Elmalili grounds rights and legitimate allegiance in God's rule."}, {"id": "3:64/q15/p6", "position": "Idols are the forbidden lords.", "reasons": "Ikrima is reported with this referent."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q16", "question": "Why say 'some of us, others' and 'besides God'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q16/p1", "position": "The reciprocal wording stresses shared humanity and the impossibility of human divinity.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan compares objections to human prophets at 14:10-11 and 23:47. Alusi limits 'our' to humans and reads 'besides' as apart from God alone; Qurtubi glosses dun as other than."}]}

{"id": "3:64/q18", "question": "What does the closing declaration demand?", "turns_on": "Explanations vary between testimony to Muslim submission, proof, reproach, indirect accusation and steadfastness.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q18/p1", "position": "Profess sincere submission and exclusive monotheism despite refusal.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari specifies inward and outward submission; Zajjaj includes prior prophets; Qurtubi rejects Jesus, Uzayr, angels and monks as lords; Tabatabai calls Islam God's approved religion."}, {"id": "3:64/q18/p2", "position": "Demand acknowledgement that proof binds them and Muslims are right.", "reasons": "Kashshaf likens it to a defeated opponent conceding; Baydawi, Nasafi and Bursevi repeat the proof-based challenge. Tabrisi says truth binds regardless of how many accept."}, {"id": "3:64/q18/p3", "position": "Publicly confront and rebuke the rejecters, warning of consequences.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reads a public announcement and threat; Abu Hayyan stresses the contrast of refusal and Muslim obedience; Biqai hears impending confrontation."}, {"id": "3:64/q18/p4", "position": "Indirectly make them admit unbelief or rejection of their own scripture.", "reasons": "Kashshaf gives an indirect challenge; Baydawi invokes their scriptures and messengers; Alusi reports verifiers preferring the implication."}, {"id": "3:64/q18/p5", "position": "Remain steadfast, openly professing Islam without fear.", "reasons": "Tabrisi names perseverance; Alusi reports this interpretation but says hiding from fear ill fits openly professing opponents."}, {"id": "3:64/q18/p6", "position": "Their testimony will stand against them at the Resurrection.", "reasons": "Bursevi compares the hadith that every hearer of the prayer call testifies for its caller."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q19", "question": "How do tawallaw and the conditional work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q19/p1", "position": "Tawallaw is past tense about opponents; faqulu addresses believers.", "reasons": "Al-Samin and Alusi reject tatwallaw because it mismatches the addressees and lacks a valid apodosis. Ibn Ashur and Biqai say 'if' portrays refusal as unlikely after the evidence."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q20", "question": "What encounter prompted or applied the invitation?", "turns_on": "Accounts place it after Najran's imprecation, among Medina Jews, in a mixed Abraham dispute, or in Abyssinia.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q20/p1", "position": "Jews and Christians disputed Abraham and alleged Muhammad wanted to be worshipped.", "reasons": "The Prophet said Abraham was a hanif; Abu Rafi and a Najranian ask whether he sought status like Jesus, and he denies it."}, {"id": "3:64/q20/p2", "position": "Najran's Christians declined imprecation and received an easier common appeal.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd names the sequence; Razi and Biqai say the Prophet continued seeking their faith after proof and tribute."}, {"id": "3:64/q20/p3", "position": "Medina Jews disputed Abraham's religion and were invited.", "reasons": "Qatada cites their claim that Abraham died a Jew and 3:65; Ibn Jurayj reports refusal, fighting and jizya."}, {"id": "3:64/q20/p4", "position": "Jafar recited the invitation before the Negus.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas connects it with priests and monks; Burhan says the Negus affirmed Abraham's faith."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q21", "question": "How was the verse used in messages to rulers?", "turns_on": "The accounts name Heraclius, other rulers, and different responses.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q21/p1", "position": "The Prophet quoted it to Heraclius in a letter inviting Islam.", "reasons": "Abu Sufyan recounts the emperor's questions and his reading of prophetic signs; the letter promises double reward and warns of subjects' sins. Roman dignitaries protested. Bukhari, Muslim and other sources transmit it."}, {"id": "3:64/q21/p2", "position": "The invitation also went to other unbelievers or rulers.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas reports letters to unbelievers; Tabatabai mentions Muqawqis and a circulated Kufic manuscript; Itqan says first Abyssinia then Rome. Al-Izz cites the letter for Quranic wording outside recitation."}, {"id": "3:64/q21/p3", "position": "Heraclius recognized signs but did not openly convert.", "reasons": "Bursevi says he feared losing his crown and wrote that he believed Muhammad a prophet but could not leave Jesus' religion; Bukhari preserves his failed test of Roman allegiance."}, {"id": "3:64/q21/p4", "position": "Khosrow tore up the Prophet's letter and lost his rule.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the envoy escaped an attempt on his life and the Prophet prayed for Khosrow's dominion to be torn apart."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q22", "question": "What happened when Najran refused mutual imprecation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q22/p1", "position": "The parties made a tribute pact after al-Aqib warned against the imprecation.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives one thousand garments in each of Safar and Rajab plus thirty old iron coats. The Prophet said imprecation would have destroyed the liars within a year; when Umar asked whose hands he would take, he named Ali, Fatima, Hasan, Husayn, Hafsa and Aisha."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q23", "question": "When could this verse have been revealed?", "turns_on": "The pre-conquest Heraclius letter conflicts with some late dates for Najran and jizya.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q23/p1", "position": "A year-nine or year-ten Najran visit implies a later revelation if it occasioned the verse.", "reasons": "Historians cited by Tabatabai give those dates; Ibn Kathir flags tension with the earlier Heraclius letter."}, {"id": "3:64/q23/p2", "position": "It was revealed twice.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir proposes before Hudaybiyya and after the conquest; Ibn Hajar transmits the possibility."}, {"id": "3:64/q23/p3", "position": "It was early, perhaps by year six or before year nine.", "reasons": "Tabatabai cites year-six letters and passage continuity; he argues Najran would not have been ignored while distant rulers were contacted."}, {"id": "3:64/q23/p4", "position": "The verse was already revealed before the wider Najran passage.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir questions the report that over eighty opening verses descended with Najran, given Abu Sufyan's earlier letter account."}, {"id": "3:64/q23/p5", "position": "Najran came before Hudaybiyya and its payment was a settlement, not jizya.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares later legislation confirming a precedent with the shares ruling after Abdullah ibn Jahsh's expedition."}, {"id": "3:64/q23/p6", "position": "The Prophet used the wording before its revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares revelation later agreeing with Umar on the veil, captives, hypocrites' funeral prayer and Abraham's station."}, {"id": "3:64/q23/p7", "position": "A reported letter before al-Naml implies a very early date, but is rejected.", "reasons": "Al-Bayhaqi transmits the letter; Tabatabai objects that al-Naml is Meccan and the jizya/war language is unexplained."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q24", "question": "What details accompany the Abyssinian recitation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q24/p1", "position": "Jafar defended Muslim migrants while the Negus heard both sides.", "reasons": "Al-Khazin's transmitted account dates Quraysh's mission after Badr: Amr and Amara brought gifts and alleged a false prophet. Jafar sought fair hearing; Muslims said they prostrated only to God and used salam. The Negus recognized their account in scripture and heard each side."}]}
{"id": "3:64/q25", "question": "How does this verse connect to its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "It follows proofs and imprecation and leads into the Abraham debate.", "positions": [{"id": "3:64/q25/p1", "position": "After proofs and refused imprecation, it returns to a gentle common appeal.", "reasons": "Razi, Baydawi, Biqai, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur cite the Prophet's concern for their faith; Ibn Ashur explains the repeated address and lack of conjunction after 3:61."}, {"id": "3:64/q25/p2", "position": "The Muslim declaration invokes Abraham's submission and prepares the next dispute.", "reasons": "Biqai cites 2:131-32 and 2:135; Ibn Ashur links Islam to Abraham's hanif faith through 16:123 and 3:67; Tabatabai calls it a new phase of address."}]}

{"id": "4:36/q01", "question": "What does worshipping God require?", "turns_on": "Whether worship here is glossed by its core of tawḥīd, by all obedient acts, or by inward self-effacement.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q01/p1", "position": "Submit humbly to God by obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions in heart and body.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Biqāʿī, and Ibn al-Jawzī connect ʿibāda with humble obedience; Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares a marked road and branded camel. Rāzī and Bursawī expressly extend it beyond monotheism to every commanded act or omission, including inward acts. Qushayrī calls it accepting commands and prohibitions; Ibn Kathīr says God's creative and providential gifts ground the duty."}, {"id": "4:36/q01/p2", "position": "Affirm God's oneness and worship Him alone.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is repeatedly reported for tawḥīd (Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn al-Jawzī, Rāzī); Muqātil contrasts this with the People of Scripture's insincere worship. Al-Ṭabrisī grounds exclusive worship in God alone giving foundational blessings."}, {"id": "4:36/q01/p3", "position": "Turn wholly toward God and become annihilated in Him.", "reasons": "Qāshānī and Ālūsī give an inward reading: exclusive orientation to God is the utmost humility."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q02", "question": "How does the form and clause structure carry the commands?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q02/p1", "position": "The first verb is an imperative with omitted plural nūn, the second a prohibition; the opening wāw coordinates clauses.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās parses the forms and Ibn ʿAṭiyya the initial conjunction; Sībawayh's general examples explain that a verb needs a subject and a nominal start its predicate."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q03", "question": "What inward meanings are given to worship and nonassociation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q03/p1", "position": "Servanthood is self-surrender through sincerity, humility, love, reverence, fear, and relinquishing self-will.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports Abū ʿUthmān on cutting attachments, Junayd on relinquishing will, Ibn ʿAṭāʾ on accepting limits, and a six-station account. Qushayrī opposes hidden self-regard and worldly praise to unity. Qāshānī and Ālūsī speak of annihilation in God; Bursawī's poem uses lā ilāha to sever other attachments and connects beneficence with divine rather than autonomous human agency, citing 32:7, 12:53 and 4:79. Reports say hidden shirk can be subtler than an ant on a dark stone; deeds without God's face become dust per 25:23."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q04", "question": "What forms of association with God does the prohibition cover?", "turns_on": "Whether the text is explained through doctrinal partners, subtle motives, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q04/p1", "position": "No created thing may share God's divinity, worship, or independent creative power.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī excludes partners in lordship and worship; al-Zajjāj says worship beside another corrupts devotion. Qurṭubī distinguishes open divine partners from claiming another independently creates, his second degree directed against Qadariyya. Asad says shayʾan includes quasi-divine powers attributed to saints or objects. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports the Prophet prohibiting shirk even under extreme torture."}, {"id": "4:36/q04/p2", "position": "The ban also includes hidden or practical association: showing off, desire, reliance on another, or mixed motives.", "reasons": "Qushayrī details ostentation, flattery, self-admiration, and praise-seeking; Sulamī reports Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and al-Wāsiṭī on relying on other than God. Qurṭubī's third degree is ostentation and his reports say God accepts only deeds intended for Him; Sahl distinguishes acting for an audience, gaining energy when seen, and delight in praise, while Qurṭubī exempts gratitude when publicity is unbidden. Ṭabāṭabāʾ reads nearby verses 4:37–39 with 38:26 and 45:23 as practical monotheism versus worship of desire. Bursawī, Kur'an Yolu, and others relate arrogance, miserliness, and praise-seeking to hidden shirk without necessarily making one a polytheist."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q05", "question": "How is shayʾan parsed, and what scope follows?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusative names a possible partner or the act of association.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q05/p1", "position": "It is the direct object: no object at all may be associated with God.", "reasons": "Ālūsī says the indefinite generalizes the ban, while ʿIṣām al-Dīn also reads the tanwīn as belittling even the smallest rival to the Necessary. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 72:2."}, {"id": "4:36/q05/p2", "position": "It substitutes for an absolute object: no degree or form of shirk is allowed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 5:42. Ālūsī applies it to open and secret shirk. Sammarrāʾī accepts both parses together, gives concrete-noun and instrument examples such as stabbing 'a knife,' and contrasts the more specified 18:110."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q06", "question": "Who are the parents in inward readings?", "turns_on": "Whether parentage is symbolic of faculties, guidance by the Prophet and Imam, or training by shaykhs.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q06/p1", "position": "They are spirit and soul, from which the heart is born.", "reasons": "Qāshānī and Ālūsī say to receive from the spirit and purify and restrain the soul's appetites. Qushayrī links their outward priority to upbringing and spiritual growth."}, {"id": "4:36/q06/p2", "position": "They include the Prophet and Ali as spiritual fathers of the community.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾ transmits ungraded reports from al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq that the verse concerned the Prophet and Ali and a report naming them two fathers; he says a guide who perfects the soul is a truer father inwardly, while bodily parents retain their outward sense."}, {"id": "4:36/q06/p3", "position": "They can signify spiritual teachers or shaykhs.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports that the disciple honors them by obedience because they know hearts; he cites Junayd giving al-Sarī's command precedence as a blessing."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q07", "question": "What kindness is owed to parents, and why are they named first?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q07/p1", "position": "Honor both parents in speech, service, support, and gentle conduct, with special priority after God's right.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās (Wāḥidī) describes lowered voice and gaze and gentle response, invoking 17:24. Rāzī cites 17:23 and 31:15, including kindness to unbelieving parents without obeying a call to shirk, and a Yemenite turned back from jihad to serve his parents. Biqāʿī, Ibn Kathīr and Rāzī ground their priority in their role as cause of one's life; Qurṭubī adduces 31:14 and a report joining divine pleasure to parental pleasure. {"id": "4:36/q08", "question": "How is iḥsānan construed with the parents?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusative is an omitted imperative's verbal noun or an exhortative construction.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q08/p1", "position": "It is an accusative verbal noun standing for an omitted command to do good.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj's grammarians, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Rāzī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾ give versions of the ellipsis; Rāzī compares 47:4. Wāḥidī reports the omitted-command analyses of al-Zajjāj and al-Farrāʾ. Ibn ʿĀshūr says fronting the object emphasizes parents without restricting goodness and takes bāʾ as respectful birr rather than financial ilā; Ālūsī lists bāʾ, ilā, and lām. Sībawayh's cited case and complementation examples distinguish accusative circumstances, predicates, and required complements."}, {"id": "4:36/q08/p2", "position": "A nominative iḥsān would be possible with the prepositional phrase as predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ permits the nominative if the verb is not expressed; Naḥḥās transmits the analysis."}, {"id": "4:36/q08/p3", "position": "It is an accusative of exhortation or an implied injunction to enjoin kindness.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī calls it an exhortative accusative and finds 'enjoin yourselves' close to his reading. {"id": "4:36/q12", "question": "Why does this verse repeat bāʾ before the kin where 2:83 does not?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q12/p1", "position": "The repeated preposition emphasizes kinship and the later recipients, especially in a sūra centrally concerned with kin.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Ālūsī contrast 2:83's Israelite context with this community's special honor. {"id": "4:36/q13", "question": "How are the listed recipients interpreted inwardly?", "turns_on": "Which inner correspondence the literal recipients evoke.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q13/p1", "position": "The near neighbor is the heart, distant neighbor the self, companion law-guided reason, and wayfarer obedient limbs.", "reasons": "Sahl al-Tustarī's scheme is transmitted by Tustarī, Sulamī and Abū Ḥayyān."}, {"id": "4:36/q13/p2", "position": "The list can map spiritual affinities, faculties, stations, and acquired virtues.", "reasons": "Qāshānī and Ālūsī identify kin with spiritual affinity, orphans with faculties cut off from spirit, needy with those lacking gnosis, neighbors by station, companion by shared station, wayfarer as truth-seeker, and owned servants as affiliated people. An alternative maps kin to immaterial spirits, orphans to spiritual faculties, needy to psychic faculties, near neighbor to intellect, distant to imagination, companion to will, wayfarer to thought, and possessions to acquired virtues."}, {"id": "4:36/q13/p3", "position": "The neighbor image obliges care for the heart, spirit, and secret.", "reasons": "Qushayrī says a house neighbor's right points inwardly to guarding the heart from corrupt thoughts, then the spirit and secret from unsuitable occupants and absence from witnessing; company with poor and orphans prepares for divine company."}, {"id": "4:36/q13/p4", "position": "The figures may signify the celestial spirit, body, heart or commanding self, and a perfected saint.", "reasons": "Ālūsī describes freeing the spirit from appetite, weaning the bodily form from desire, guiding the heart's longing, restraining the self, and guarding and obeying the saint. A report calls the self between one's sides one's worst enemy."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q14", "question": "Who are the orphans and why and how should they be cared for?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q14/p1", "position": "A fatherless child before maturity deserves gentle care, support, and protection of property.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Māwardī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya define the orphan by loss of the father before puberty; Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports both a puberty limit and Ibn ʿAbbās's sound-judgment criterion from 4:6. Ibn ʿAbbās urges closeness, stroking the head, upbringing, and guarding assets. Rāzī, Biqāʿī and Ibn Kathīr stress youth and lack of a provider; reports in Baghawī and Durr promise closeness to the Prophet in Paradise for caring for an orphan. Ṭabrisī and Bursawī specify property management and spending in the child's best interest."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q15", "question": "Who are the needy and what kindness is due to them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q15/p1", "position": "People humbled by unmet needs deserve provision, charity, or a kind answer.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Māwardī connect miskīn with the abasement of need; Ibn Kathīr requires help until hardship is relieved. Wāḥidī, Rāzī, Bursawī and Wajīz allow a modest gift or courteous refusal, citing 93:10. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports that the truly poor may refrain from asking and go unnoticed, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya specifies indigent Muslims visibly asking and eligible for zakat. Rāzī contrasts an adult's ability to ask with an orphan's helplessness, explaining the order."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q16", "question": "Who is the near neighbor?", "turns_on": "Whether qurbā marks kinship, residential proximity, religious or communal nearness, or a particular grammatical annexation.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q16/p1", "position": "A neighbor who is also a blood relative.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda and many others are reported for this sense by Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Kathīr and later commentators. Qatāda gives that person both kinship and neighborhood rights; Wāḥidī adds Islamic rights. Wāḥidī prefers this majority interpretation, and Ṭabarī argues ordinary Arabic qurbā denotes blood kinship."}, {"id": "4:36/q16/p2", "position": "A neighbor whose home is physically near or who is familiar to you.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj stresses mutual acquaintance; Wāḥidī says the contrast with the distant neighbor supports proximity despite preferring blood kinship. Spatial interpreters cite ʿĀʾisha's nearer-door gift report. Ibn ʿAshūr rejects this because he says qurbā does not denote spatial proximity; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects Maymūn's particular grammatical construction. Some sources give both spatial and kinship options."}, {"id": "4:36/q16/p3", "position": "A Muslim neighbor, near through religion.", "reasons": "Nawf al-Shāmī contrasts Muslim with Jewish or Christian neighbor; other commentators report it. Ṭabarī argues against reading religious nearness because ordinary Arabic usage points to blood relationship."}, {"id": "4:36/q16/p4", "position": "The neighbor of a relative, bound to you through that relative.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī reports Maymūn ibn Mihrān, but Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya reject the definite article with this intended annexation; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn rescue it by positing an omitted appositive noun."}, {"id": "4:36/q16/p5", "position": "A wife, the closest neighbor.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Kathīr report this from ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī cite poetry calling a wife the closest neighbor."}, {"id": "4:36/q16/p6", "position": "A person from one's own community rather than an actual relative.", "reasons": "Asad says kin already have their own place earlier in the list; he contrasts another community in the next expression."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q17", "question": "What duties are owed to neighbors?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q17/p1", "position": "Care for every neighbor, share help and food, and protect them from harm, whatever their faith.", "reasons": "The Prophet's Gabriel report, transmitted in Baghawī, Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and Durr, says the urging was so strong he thought neighbors would inherit. Other reports tie faith to a neighbor's safety, rank adultery or theft against a neighbor especially grave, and urge broth sharing. Thaʿlabī, Rāzī, Qurṭubī and Bursawī list aid, lending, invitations, visiting illness, condolences, funerals and avoiding harmful building. Qurṭubī notes the comprehensive rights report is ḥasan despite a disapproved transmitter. Reports grant Muslim kin three rights, Muslim nonkin two, and non-Muslims neighborliness; Ālūsī calls that route weak and Kur'an Yolu uncertain, while broader sound reports have no religious restriction. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees the duty as perfecting an Arab virtue; Kur'an Yolu ties it to equal civic treatment, invoking 5:8."}]}

{"id": "4:36/q19", "question": "Which neighbor should receive a gift first?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q19/p1", "position": "The neighbor whose door is closer.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha's question receives this answer in Bukhārī as cited by Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr, Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and others. {"id": "4:36/q20", "question": "Must an owner allow a neighbor to place a beam or watercourse through the property?", "turns_on": "Whether the Prophetic beam command creates an enforceable amenity or recommends generosity subject to property consent.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q20/p1", "position": "Yes, a harmless neighbor amenity is obligatory.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, Dāwūd and hadith scholars taking the beam command as binding; Abū Hurayra insists on it. ʿUmar forced passage of a watercourse, and al-Shāfiʿī argues no Companion opposed him. Earlier jurists distinguish use of an amenity from transfer or consumption of property; a Medinan judge reportedly ruled for this right."}, {"id": "4:36/q20/p2", "position": "No, it is recommended kindness and the owner's consent remains decisive.", "reasons": "Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa appeal to inviolability of property. {"id": "4:36/q21", "question": "Do neighbor rights confer property preemption or determine bequests?", "turns_on": "Whether neighborliness implies a proprietary claim, and how broadly 'neighbor' in a bequest is construed.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q21/p1", "position": "A neighbor may have a preemption claim from proximity.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports scholars drawing on the nearer-door gift report and a report of a neighbor's claim to adjoining property."}, {"id": "4:36/q21/p2", "position": "The gift report establishes priority in giving, not preemption.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī rejects the inference because ʿĀʾisha asked only whom to gift first; Abū Ḥanīfa denies preemption without shared wall or route if the adjoining neighbor waives it."}, {"id": "4:36/q21/p3", "position": "A bequest to neighbors includes adjoining and other nearby neighbors.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports this as the majority view."}, {"id": "4:36/q21/p4", "position": "A bequest to neighbors reaches only the adjoining neighbor.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī attributes this restriction to Abū Ḥanīfa."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q22", "question": "How is the near neighbor read and parsed?", "turns_on": "Genitive coordination versus accusative exhortation or specification.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q22/p1", "position": "Ibn Abī ʿAbla, sometimes with Abū Ḥaywa, reads the neighbor in the accusative; dhā may mark specification.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya report the reading, Jishumī calls it an exhortation, and Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Ālūsī explain specification as exalting a neighbor's joint kinship and neighborhood claim, comparing 2:238."}, {"id": "4:36/q22/p2", "position": "The common reading makes the neighbor genitive, coordinated with the preceding recipients.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī and Jishumī name the common reading."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q23", "question": "Who is the distant neighbor?", "turns_on": "Whether junub describes kinship, faith, household distance, or social association.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q23/p1", "position": "An unrelated or foreign neighbor, distant in kinship or lineage.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers a nonrelative of any religion, Muslim or otherwise, as the counterpart of the kin-neighbor. Al-Akhfash, Abū ʿUbayda, Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn ʿĀshūr derive junub from separation or distance; verses of ʿAlqama, al-Aʿshā and Bulʿāʾ b. Qays illustrate a stranger. The junub person's separation from prayer until washing and 14:35 are additional analogies; some analyze junub as an adjective, others as a verbal noun."}, {"id": "4:36/q23/p2", "position": "A non-Muslim neighbor, especially a Jew or Christian, distant in religion.", "reasons": "Nawf al-Shāmī supplies the Jew-or-Christian explanation; Māwardī broadens to a non-Muslim. Qurṭubī explicitly says the duty includes Muslims and non-Muslims, and Kur'an Yolu reports his approval of this reading."}, {"id": "4:36/q23/p3", "position": "A neighbor whose home is farther away.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and other spatial readings contrast near and far houses; Ṭabāṭabāʾ suggests reports of forty cubits and forty houses might mark the two ranges. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects spatial qurbā as Arabic usage."}, {"id": "4:36/q23/p4", "position": "A neighbor from another people or community.", "reasons": "Muqātil and reports from Qatāda and Mujāhid express this as a foreign community; Asad makes it the opposite of a neighbor from one's own community."}, {"id": "4:36/q23/p5", "position": "A neighbor who lodges near enough to be seen, including an adjoining neighbor.", "reasons": "Abū Makūza (in Naḥḥās) describes someone settling in sight; Thaʿlabī reports the adjoining-house reading, and Abū Ḥayyān quotes a Bedouin's formulation."}, {"id": "4:36/q23/p6", "position": "A travel companion sharing lodging and close company.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Kathīr transmit this explanation from Mujāhid."}, {"id": "4:36/q23/p7", "position": "A man's wife.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits an unnamed Companion's interpretation through Makkī and Ibn Wahb."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q24", "question": "May sacrificial meat be shared with a non-Muslim neighbor?", "turns_on": "Whether the sacrifice is obligatory or voluntary.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q24/p1", "position": "A protected non-Muslim neighbor may receive nonobligatory sacrificial meat.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports the Prophet telling ʿĀʾisha to begin with their Jewish neighbor and ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr repeatedly asking whether meat was sent to his Jewish neighbor."}, {"id": "4:36/q24/p2", "position": "The prohibition on feeding polytheists applies to obligatory sacrificial meat.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī records a contrary Prophetic answer about Muslim sacrifices but construes it as an obligatory sacrifice, which also may not feed its performer or the wealthy."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q25", "question": "How is honoring a guest connected with the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q25/p1", "position": "Hospitality is part of the same moral care enjoined toward neighbors, companions, and travelers.", "reasons": "Burhān connects the saying to honor guests with Abraham's honored guests and this verse, citing 51:24; it adds guarding secrets, preventing harm, speaking well or remaining silent, and neighborly kindness."}]}
{"id": "4:36/q26", "question": "What is the form of junub in the distant-neighbor phrase?", "turns_on": "Whether the invariant descriptive form is adjectival or a verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q26/p1", "position": "It is an adjective on the faʿl or fuʿl pattern, meaning separated or distant.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī, Wāḥidī, al-Samīn and Ibn ʿĀshūr treat it as an adjective; al-Samīn notes invariance across gender and number and occasional inflection. {"id": "4:36/q27", "question": "How is al-junub pronounced?", "turns_on": "Two attested vocalizations and how the second is analyzed.", "positions": [{"id": "4:36/q27/p1", "position": "Al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim, and reports from al-Aʿmash or al-Faḍl, have fatḥa on jīm and sukūn on nūn.", "reasons": "The sources call both forms Arabic dialects.
